docs.title: URL Shortener
docs.text: # URL Shortener System Design

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Design a scalable URL shortening service.

docs.title: URL Shortener — Q&A
docs.text: A Q&A style reference for the URL Shortener system design.

docs.title: Q1: What is a URL Shortener?
docs.text:
Front: What is a URL Shortener? Back: Answer: A URL Shortener is a service that converts a long URL into a short, unique, and easily shareable URL. Example: 

Original: https://www.example.com/articles/2025/long-article-title  
Short: https://short.ly/abc123

docs.title: Q2: What are the key features of a URL Shortener?
docs.text: Answer: 1. Generate unique short URLs. 2. Redirect users from short URL to the original long URL. 3. Track usage analytics (optional). 4. Handle collisions gracefully. 5. Support custom aliases (optional).

docs.title: Q3: What are the main components of a URL Shortener system?
docs.text: Answer: 1. API Server — Accepts requests to create or retrieve URLs. 2. Database — Stores the mapping between short and long URLs. 3. Cache — (Optional) For faster redirection using systems like Redis. 4. Hashing / Encoding Logic — Converts long URL to short key. 5. Frontend / Dashboard — Optional UI for users.

docs.title: Q4: How do you generate a unique short URL key?
docs.text:
Answer: - Hashing the long URL (e.g., MD5, SHA) → Base62 encoded. - Random string generation (6-8 characters). - Incremental ID → encode to Base62.

Considerations: - Avoid collisions. - Make the key short and URL-friendly. - Optionally allow custom aliases.

docs.title: Q5: How to handle collisions?
docs.text: Answer: - Check the database if the generated key already exists. - If yes, regenerate a new key (loop until unique). - Use probabilistic approaches (like using longer keys for high volume).

docs.title: Q6: What databases can we use?
docs.text: Answer: - Relational DBs: MySQL, PostgreSQL — easy mapping with unique constraints. - NoSQL: DynamoDB, MongoDB — good for scalability. - In-memory cache: Redis or Memcached — for fast redirection.

docs.title: Q7: How to scale a URL Shortener?
docs.text: Answer: 1. Database Sharding — Distribute the mappings across multiple DBs. 2. Caching — Use Redis to store hot keys. 3. Load Balancing — Multiple API servers. 4. CDN for redirect — Optional for global low-latency redirection.

docs.title: Q8: How to ensure high availability?
docs.text: Answer: - Use replicated databases. - Multi-zone deployment of API servers. - Backup and restore strategies for URL mappings.

docs.title: Q9: What security considerations exist?
docs.text: Answer: - Validate long URLs to prevent phishing/malware. - Rate-limit API requests. - Use HTTPS for all short URLs. - Optional: authentication for creating custom URLs.

docs.title: Q10: Optional enhancements
docs.text: Answer: - Expiration time for short URLs. - Analytics dashboard: clicks, geography, referrer. - Custom vanity URLs. - QR code generation.

"While I am doing my work, what changes from others am I allowed to see?"

Transactions do NOT run one after another. They run together, but isolation controls what they can see.

docs.title: 2. Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction is a group of steps that must happen together.

Example:

BEGIN
  Read balance
  Update balance
COMMIT

Either all steps succeed or none of them apply.

docs.title: 3. Problems That Happen Without Proper Isolation (Anomalies)
docs.text: Before learning isolation levels, understand these problems.

docs.title: What it means
docs.text: You read data before the other person finishes their work.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Initial balance = 100

T1 (Transaction 1)           T2 (Transaction 2)
------------------           ------------------
UPDATE balance = 0
                              READ balance → 0 ❌
ROLLBACK

Final balance is still 100, but T2 saw 0, which never actually existed.

📌 This is called a Dirty Read

docs.title: What it means
docs.text: You read the same row twice and get different values.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
T1                           T2
------------------           ------------------
READ balance → 100
                              UPDATE balance = 200
                              COMMIT
READ balance → 200 ❌

T1 is confused: "I didn’t change anything, why did my data change?"

📌 This is a Non‑Repeatable Read

docs.title: 3.3 Phantom Read (New Rows Appear Like Ghosts)
What it means
docs.text: You run the same query twice, but the number of rows changes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
T1                           T2
------------------           ------------------
SELECT COUNT(*)
WHERE salary > 50k → 2
                              INSERT salary = 70k
                              COMMIT
SELECT COUNT(*)
WHERE salary > 50k → 3 ❌

Rows appeared out of nowhere.

📌 This is a Phantom Read

docs.title: What it means
docs.text: Two people make individually correct updates, but together they break a rule.

docs.title: Example (Doctor On‑Call Rule)
docs.text:
Rule: At least one doctor must be on call

T1                           T2
------------------           ------------------
READ A=ON, B=ON              READ A=ON, B=ON
SET A=OFF                    SET B=OFF
COMMIT                       COMMIT

Final state:

A = OFF
B = OFF ❌  (Rule broken)

📌 This happens even though no row conflict occurred.

docs.title: 4. Isolation Levels (Big Picture)
docs.text:
Think of isolation levels as rules that block some of the problems above.

Isolation Level Dirty Read Non‑Repeatable Phantom Write Skew READ UNCOMMITTED ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌ READ COMMITTED ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌ REPEATABLE READ ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌ SERIALIZABLE ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

docs.title: Idea
docs.text: "Read anything, even unfinished work."

docs.title: What happens
docs.text:
• Dirty reads allowed

  • Data can be totally wrong

📌 Most real databases don’t even allow this.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text: "Only read committed data, but data may change later."

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
T1                           T2
------------------           ------------------
READ balance → 100
                              UPDATE balance = 200
                              COMMIT
READ balance → 200  (allowed)

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Each query gets a fresh view of committed data.

📌 Default in PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server

docs.title: Idea
docs.text: "Once I read something, it should not change for me."

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
T1                           T2
------------------           ------------------
READ balance → 100
                              UPDATE balance = 200
                              COMMIT
READ balance → 100  (same)

docs.title: But Phantom Reads?
docs.text:
T1                           T2
------------------           ------------------
COUNT salary > 50k → 2
                              INSERT salary = 70k
                              COMMIT
COUNT salary > 50k → 3 ❌

📌 Snapshot stays same for rows, not for ranges (DB‑dependent)

docs.title: Idea
docs.text: "Behave as if transactions ran one after another."

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
T1 runs fully
then
T2 runs fully

docs.title: How DBs Actually Do This
docs.text:
• They don’t block everything immediately

  • They detect conflicts

  • They may abort one transaction

📌 Safest but slowest

docs.title: 9. Snapshot Isolation (Reality Check)
docs.text: Most databases actually use snapshots, not pure locking.

docs.title: What Snapshot Means
docs.text: "I see the database as it was when I started."

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Snapshot isolation does NOT stop write skew.

That’s why:

REPEATABLE READ ≠ SERIALIZABLE

"Isolation controls which concurrency problems are allowed. Most systems use Read Committed for performance. Serializable is used only when correctness is critical because it may abort transactions."

docs.title: 10. One‑Line Memory Trick
docs.text:
• Dirty Read → Reading unfinished work

  • Non‑Repeatable → Same row changes

  • Phantom → Row count changes

  • Write Skew → Rule broken without conflict

docs.title: 11. Final Takeaway
docs.text:
Isolation is a trade‑off:

  • Higher isolation → safer but slower

  • Lower isolation → faster but risky

choose isolation based on business rules, not defaults.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text: A Non-Relational Database (NoSQL) is a database that does not use the traditional relational table-based structure (rows and columns with fixed schema). NoSQL databases are designed for: - Large-scale data storage - Distributed systems - High availability - Flexible schema - Horizontal scalability NoSQL databases typically follow BASE consistency rather than strict ACID transactions.

docs.title: 2. Characteristics of NoSQL Databases
docs.text:
• Schema-less or flexible schema
  • Horizontally scalable (scale-out architecture)
  • Designed for distributed systems
  • High read/write performance
  • Supports unstructured and semi-structured data

docs.title: 3. Types of NoSQL Databases
docs.text: There are four main types: 1. Key–Value Stores 2. Document Databases 3. Column-Family (Wide Column) Databases 4. Graph Databases

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A Key–Value database stores data in the form: Key → Value The database treats the value as an opaque object.

docs.title: Structure Example
docs.text: User123 → {Name: Rahul, Age: 22}

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Very fast lookups
  • Simple structure
  • Highly scalable

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• O(1) lookup by key
  • Simple design
  • Excellent for caching

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No complex querying
  • No joins
  • Cannot search inside value (in most cases)

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Session storage
  • Caching
  • User preferences
  • Shopping carts

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Redis
  • Amazon DynamoDB

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A Document database stores data in documents (usually JSON or BSON format). Each document: - Has unique ID - Contains key-value pairs - Can have nested objects - Does not require fixed schema

docs.title: Structure Example
docs.text: { "id": 1, "name": "Rahul", "skills": ["Java", "Python"], "address": { "city": "Bangalore" } }

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Flexible schema
  • Supports indexing
  • Supports rich queries

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Easy to modify structure
  • Good for evolving applications
  • Developer-friendly

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Limited join support
  • Data duplication possible

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• E-commerce websites
  • Content management systems
  • User profile systems

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• MongoDB
  • CouchDB

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Data is stored in column families instead of rows. Unlike relational databases: - Each row can have different columns - Columns are grouped into families - Optimized for distributed storage

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• High write performance
  • Massive scalability
  • Distributed architecture

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Handles huge data volumes
  • Suitable for big data
  • Good for time-series data

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Complex data modeling
  • Limited transactional support

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Logging systems
  • IoT data
  • Analytics platforms
  • Real-time big data processing

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Apache Cassandra
  • Apache HBase

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Graph databases store data as: - Nodes (Entities) - Edges (Relationships) - Properties (Attributes) Designed to efficiently handle highly connected data.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Relationship-first model
  • Fast graph traversal
  • No complex joins needed

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Efficient for multi-level relationships
  • Natural modeling of connected systems
  • Good for network analysis

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Not ideal for heavy aggregation
  • Overkill for simple CRUD apps

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Social networks
  • Fraud detection
  • Recommendation systems
  • Knowledge graphs

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Neo4j
  • Amazon Neptune

docs.title: ACID (Used in RDBMS)
docs.text:
• Atomicity
  • Consistency
  • Isolation
  • Durability Ensures strong transactional guarantees.

docs.title: BASE (Used in NoSQL)
docs.text:
• Basically Available
  • Soft State
  • Eventually Consistent Prioritizes availability and scalability over strict consistency.

docs.title: 5. CAP Theorem
docs.text: CAP theorem states that a distributed system can guarantee only two of the following three: - Consistency - Availability - Partition Tolerance Most NoSQL systems choose: - AP (Availability + Partition tolerance) or - CP (Consistency + Partition tolerance)

docs.title: 6. Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling
docs.text: Vertical Scaling: - Add more power (CPU, RAM) to single server. Horizontal Scaling: - Add more servers. - Data is distributed using sharding. NoSQL databases are designed for horizontal scaling.

docs.title: 7. Sharding
docs.text: Sharding is horizontal partitioning of data across multiple servers to distribute load and improve performance. Example: Users 1–1000 → Server A Users 1001–2000 → Server B

docs.title: 8. Comparison Table
docs.text: Feature Key-Value Document Column-Family Graph Structure Key → Value JSON Document Column Families Nodes & Edges Schema None Flexible Semi-structured Flexible Query Power Low Medium-High Medium High (relationships) Best For Caching Web apps Big data Connected data

docs.title: 9. Advantages of NoSQL
docs.text:
• High scalability
  • Handles big data
  • Flexible schema
  • High availability
  • Faster development

docs.title: 10. Disadvantages of NoSQL
docs.text:
• Limited transactions
  • No complex joins
  • Data redundancy
  • Eventual consistency issues

docs.title: 1) What is NoSQL?
docs.text: NoSQL is a non-relational database designed for distributed data storage, flexible schema, and horizontal scalability.

docs.title: 2) When should you use NoSQL?
docs.text:
• When handling big data
  • When schema changes frequently
  • When high scalability is required
  • When joins are not needed

docs.title: 3) What is eventual consistency?
docs.text: Data updates will propagate to all nodes over time but not immediately.

docs.title: 4) What is sharding?
docs.text: Sharding is splitting data across multiple machines to improve scalability.

docs.title: 5) Difference between MongoDB and Cassandra?
docs.text: MongoDB is a document database, while Cassandra is a column-family database optimized for large distributed systems.

docs.title: 6) What problems are graph databases best at?
docs.text: Path finding, recommendation systems, fraud detection, and social networks.

docs.title: 12. Short Exam Definition (4–5 lines)
docs.text: Non-Relational databases (NoSQL) are distributed, schema-flexible databases designed for large-scale and high-performance applications. The main types are Key-Value, Document, Column-Family, and Graph databases. They typically follow BASE consistency and scale horizontally across multiple servers.

docs.title: 1. What is Data?
docs.text:
Data is raw information that represents facts, observations, or measurements. Examples:

  • A name: Ram
  • A number: 25
  • A date: 2026-01-10
  • A status: DONE

By itself, data has limited value. Its real value comes when it is stored, structured, and queried efficiently.

docs.title: 2. What is a Database?
docs.text:
A database is an organized collection of data that allows:

  • Storing data permanently
  • Reading data efficiently
  • Updating data safely
  • Deleting data when required Instead of storing data in files (like text files or Excel), databases provide:
  • Faster access
  • Data safety
  • Concurrency (multiple users at the same time)
  • Reliability

docs.title: 3. How is Data Stored in Relational Databases?
docs.text:
In a Relational Database, data is stored in tables.

Table Structure

  • Rows → Individual records
  • Columns → Attributes (fields)

Example: Users Table

id name email age 1 Ram ram@gmail.com 25 2 Amit amit@gmail.com 28
  • Each row represents one user
  • Each column represents a property of the user

docs.title: 4. What is a Relational Database (RDBMS)?
docs.text:
A Relational Database is a database that:

  • Stores data in tables
  • Establishes relationships between tables
  • Uses keys (Primary Key, Foreign Key) to maintain these relationships

Example of Relationship

Orders Table

order_id user_id amount 101 1 500 102 2 300

Here: - user_id refers to Users.id - This creates a relationship between Users and Orders

docs.title: 5.1 Data Consistency
docs.text:
Data remains correct and reliable across the database.

Example:

  • If a user balance is ₹1000, it should not show ₹800 in another query unless updated properly.

docs.title: 5.2 Data Durability
docs.text:
Once data is committed, it will not be lost, even if:

  • The system crashes
  • Power goes off

Databases achieve this using:

  • Write‑Ahead Logs (WAL)
  • Disk persistence

docs.title: 5.3 Data Integrity
docs.text:
Ensures data is accurate and valid.

Types of integrity:

  • Entity Integrity – Primary key cannot be NULL
  • Referential Integrity – Foreign key must refer to existing data
  • Domain Integrity – Data must follow rules (age > 0)

docs.title: 5.4 Constraints
docs.text:
Constraints are rules enforced by the database.

Common constraints:

  • PRIMARY KEY
  • FOREIGN KEY
  • UNIQUE
  • NOT NULL
  • CHECK

Example:

age INT CHECK (age >= 18)

docs.title: 5.5 Everything in One Place (Centralized Source of Truth)
docs.text:
• All data lives in a single system
  • Prevents duplication
  • Avoids conflicts between multiple data copies

This makes RDBMS ideal for enterprise systems.

docs.title: 6. Why Do Relational Databases Support Transactions?
docs.text:
Because of the above properties, RDBMS supports transactions.

A transaction is a group of operations that must execute completely or not at all.

Example:

  • Deduct money from Account A
  • Add money to Account B

Both must succeed, or both must fail.

docs.title: 7. ACID Properties
docs.text:
ACID guarantees safe and reliable transactions. ACID = Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability

A transaction is a logical unit of work that contains one or more database operations. Example: Transfer ₹100 from Account A to Account B This involves multiple steps but must behave as one unit.

docs.title: 7.1 Atomicity
docs.text:
• All operations succeed or none do - All or Nothing

Example: Steps in a transaction: 1. Deduct ₹100 from Account A 2. Add ₹100 to Account B

docs.title: Possible Outcomes:
docs.text:
• Both steps succeed → ✅ Transaction committed
  • Any step fails → ❌ Entire transaction rolled back

❌ Not allowed:

  • Money deducted from A but not added to B

How Databases Achieve Atomicity - Use undo logs / rollback logs - If a failure occurs, changes are reverted to the previous state

Real-World Analogy Think of an ATM transaction: - Either you get cash and your balance is reduced - Or you get nothing and your balance remains unchanged

docs.title: 7.2 Consistency
docs.text:
Always Valid State Consistency ensures that a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state, following all rules and constraints. What “Rules” Mean Rules include: - Primary keys - Foreign keys - Unique constraints - Check constraints - Business rules Example: Constraint: balance >= 0 Transaction: Withdraw ₹500 from account with ₹300 ❌ Result: - Balance becomes -200 → violates constraint

➡️ Transaction is rejected ➡️ Database remains consistent Important Clarification - Consistency is not about concurrency - It is about data correctness

Real-World Analogy A form submission: - Age field must be a number - Email must be valid If rules fail → submission rejected - Database moves from one valid state to another - Constraints are always respected

docs.title: 7.3 Isolation
docs.text:
Transactions Don’t Interfere Isolation ensures that multiple transactions running at the same time do not affect each other’s intermediate states.

Each transaction behaves as if it is the only one running.

docs.title: Why Isolation Is Needed
docs.text:
In real systems: - Thousands of users - Many transactions running concurrently Without isolation → data corruption

Example: Initial balance: ₹1000 Two transactions run at the same time: - T1: Withdraw ₹300 - T2: Withdraw ₹500 ❌ Without isolation: - Both read balance as ₹1000 - Final balance becomes wrong ✅ With isolation: - Transactions are properly ordered or controlled - Final balance is correct Isolation Problems It Prevents - Dirty Reads – reading uncommitted data - Non-repeatable Reads - Phantom Reads

Isolation Levels (Brief) - Read Uncommitted - Read Committed - Repeatable Read - Serializable (strongest)

Higher isolation = more safety, less concurrency

Real-World Analogy Two people editing the same Google Doc: - Changes are managed so work doesn’t conflict incorrectly

docs.title: 7.4 Durability
docs.text:
Once Committed, Never Lost Durability guarantees that once a transaction is committed, its changes will survive system crashes, power failures, or restarts.

Example: - Transaction committed - Server crashes immediately after ✅ After restart: - Data is still present

docs.title: How Databases Achieve Durability
docs.text:
• Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
  • Persistent storage (disk, SSD)
  • Replication

Important Point Durability applies only after COMMIT. Before commit: - Data can be lost After commit: - Data must persist

Real-World Analogy Once you receive a payment confirmation, the transaction is recorded permanently—even if the app crashes afterward.

docs.title: 8. When to Choose a Relational Database?
docs.text:
Pick an RDBMS when:

  • Data has clear relationships
  • You need ACID transactions
  • Data correctness is critical

  • Strong consistency is required Common Use Cases

  • Banking systems

  • Order management systems
  • Inventory systems
  • Enterprise applications

docs.title: 9. Popular Relational Databases
docs.text:
• MySQL
  • PostgreSQL
  • Oracle
  • SQL Server

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text:
Relational Databases: - Store data in tables - Maintain relationships - Enforce constraints and integrity - Support transactions using ACID

They are best suited for systems where data correctness, reliability, and consistency matter more than flexibility.
End of Notes

docs.title: Partitioning
docs.text:
Dividing a dataset into smaller logical pieces. - Vertical partitioning → Split by columns - Horizontal partitioning → Split by rows

Sharding = horizontal partitioning across multiple machines.

docs.title: Problems Without Sharding
docs.text:
• Vertical scaling limit (CPU, RAM, Disk)
  • Single point of failure
  • Write throughput bottleneck
  • Large index degradation

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Horizontal scalability
  • Higher write throughput
  • Fault isolation
  • Reduced index size per node

docs.title: A) Vertical Partitioning
docs.text: Split by columns. Example: User table: (id, name, email) → Table A (profile_pic, bio) → Table B Used for: - Reducing I/O - Separating hot vs cold data

docs.title: B) Horizontal Partitioning (Sharding)
docs.text: Split rows across shards: Shard 1 → user_id 1–1M Shard 2 → user_id 1M–2M

docs.title: 4.1 Range-Based Sharding
docs.text: Partition by value range. Example: 0–1000 → Shard 1 1001–2000 → Shard 2

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• Efficient range queries
  • Simple routing

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Hotspot risk
  • Uneven distribution
  • Difficult resharding

docs.title: 4.2 Hash-Based Sharding
docs.text: shard_id = hash(key) % N

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• Uniform distribution
  • Avoids skew (generally)

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Poor for range queries
  • Adding shard → full rehash

docs.title: 4.3 Consistent Hashing (High-Value Topic)
docs.text: Used in: - Apache Cassandra - Amazon DynamoDB - Redis Cluster

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text:
• Map nodes + keys on hash ring
  • Key assigned to next clockwise node

docs.title: Key Advantage
docs.text: When adding/removing node: - Only small portion of keys move - No global rehash

docs.title: > Consistent hashing minimizes key redistribution during cluster scaling.
Shard Key Selection (Extremely Important)
docs.text: Bad shard key = production disaster.

docs.title: Good Shard Key Properties
docs.text:
• High cardinality
  • Uniform distribution
  • Frequently used in queries
  • Immutable
  • Avoid monotonic growth

docs.title: Bad Examples
docs.text:
• country → low cardinality
  • created_at → hotspot on latest shard
  • Boolean fields

docs.title: Good Examples
docs.text:
• user_id
  • order_id
  • UUID

docs.title: Hotspot Problem
docs.text: Even with hashing: - Celebrity accounts - Trending content - Write-heavy users

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
• Key salting
  • Logical partitioning
  • Caching (e.g., Redis)
  • Write spreading
  • Rate limiting

docs.title: Rebalancing
docs.text: Triggered when: - Adding/removing shards - Skew detection - Storage threshold exceeded

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
• Data migration cost
  • Network congestion
  • Replica lag
  • Temporary performance drop Modern DBs rebalance gradually.

docs.title: Sharding + Replication
docs.text:
Sharding ≠ Replication

Concept Purpose Sharding Scale Replication Availability

Example: Each shard has: - 1 Primary - 2 Replicas Used in: - MongoDB - MySQL - PostgreSQL

docs.title: Cross-Shard Queries
docs.text: Single-shard query: SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id = X Cross-shard query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount > 1000 Requires: - Scatter-gather - Merge results - Global sort

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
• High latency
  • Expensive
  • Hard to maintain strong consistency

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
• Denormalization
  • Secondary indexes
  • Data duplication
  • Analytics DB separate

docs.title: Distributed Transactions
docs.text:
Across shards: - Require 2PC (Two-Phase Commit) - Slow - Complex - Reduce availability

Systems: - Google Spanner → Strong consistency - Apache Cassandra → Tunable consistency

Interview Tip: Avoid cross-shard transactions in design unless necessary.

docs.title: CAP Theorem Context
docs.text: In distributed sharded systems: Must tolerate network partitions. Tradeoff between: - Consistency - Availability Most NoSQL systems favor:

docs.title: Directory-Based Sharding
docs.text: Instead of computing shard: Maintain lookup table: user_id → shard_id

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• Flexible
  • Easy resharding

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Directory becomes bottleneck
  • Extra lookup cost

docs.title: Geo-Sharding
docs.text: Partition by region: India users → India cluster US users → US cluster Used for: - Data locality - Compliance (GDPR) - Low latency

docs.title: Q1: Why not vertical scaling?
docs.text: Hardware limit + cost + SPOF.

docs.title: Q2: What happens when a shard fills?
docs.text: Resharding or data migration.

docs.title: Q3: Can we change shard key?
docs.text: Yes, but extremely expensive migration.

docs.title: Q4: Why avoid cross-shard joins?
docs.text: Require coordination → latency + complexity.

docs.title: Q5: How do you handle uneven traffic?
docs.text: Rebalancing + virtual nodes + caching.

docs.title: Quick Comparison
docs.text: Strategy Uniform Range Queries Easy Scaling Range ❌ ✅ ❌ Hash ✅ ❌ ❌ Consistent Hash ✅ ❌ ✅

docs.title: Practical Design Heuristics
docs.text:
• Shard by access pattern, not by intuition.
  • Keep related data in same shard.
  • Avoid cross-shard transactions.
  • Replication factor ≥ 3.
  • Monitor shard size & QPS.
  • Plan resharding from day 1.
